speaker: Boaz Weinstein
title: Boaz Weinstein on the Money Stuff Podcast
question: When a publicly traded BDC or closed-end credit fund trades at a 50% discount to NAV, why do managers keep originating new loans instead of buying back shares?
guest: I watched a conference call where an analyst from another fund asked so gently—I'm going to paraphrase: "Your fund is trading at a 50% discount to book. You have some loans that came due and paid your money back, and you got coupons in. Why do you continue to make new investments when you can buy back your portfolio at a 50% discount?" If the NAV is right, that is a 100% guaranteed return. If the NAV is wrong and shouldn't be at 100, it should be at 80, it is a 60% guaranteed return—compared to making a new loan at 11% or 13%. So what is really going on is you don't want your fund, which has a NAV of $5.6 billion but is trading at $2.8 billion, to shrink because you are paid fees on NAV. When you invest in these funds at this discount, they are paid their fee on basically twice the price. They don't want to shrink. When they don't go into the market and buy back shares at a 50% discount, which is 100% to the upside, because they want to make a new loan at 12%, greed is laid bare.

points.core: Repurchasing shares at half of NAV offers far higher returns than new loans.
points.note: Accept: buying back shares at a 50% discount yields a 100% immediate return if NAV holds (or ~60% even if NAV is 20% overstated), dwarfing ~11%–13% yields on new loans. Do not credit: vague statements that buybacks are accretive.

points.core: Managers earn fees on reported NAV rather than the fund's market capitalization.
points.note: Accept: management fee bases tied to book NAV or gross assets, meaning managers collect fees on effectively double the market value at a 50% discount. Do not credit: generic claims that managers are greedy without explaining the fee base.

points.core: Buying back shares shrinks the fund's asset base, directly cutting manager fee revenue.
points.note: Accept: managers refusing to shrink AUM because share repurchases permanently reduce managed assets and ongoing fee income. Do not credit: generic mentions of misaligned incentives without linking to AUM shrinkage.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Mostly because of incentives, reinforced by real constraints. External managers are paid a base fee on gross assets (often 1–1.5%, including leveraged assets) plus incentive fees on income. Buying back shares shrinks the asset base and therefore the fee stream, while originating loans preserves or grows it. The buyback's benefit goes to shareholders; the cost falls on the manager.

There are also legitimate obstacles. A 50% discount usually signals that the market disbelieves the stated NAV or expects credit losses, and in that situation the fund is often tight on liquidity. Buybacks reduce equity, raising leverage toward the regulatory asset-coverage limit (150% for most BDCs) and toward credit facility covenants, just when lenders and rating agencies want a cushion. BDCs must also distribute roughly 90% of taxable income to keep RIC status, so there's little retained cash; repurchases would have to be funded by selling illiquid loans, possibly below their marks, or by repayments. Managers also cite the need to fund existing commitments, preserve sponsor relationships, and maintain scale and trading liquidity.

Weak governance lets the conflict persist: boards are typically manager-aligned, and activists face structural hurdles.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Managers are deterred by both misaligned incentives and binding balance-sheet constraints. Most BDCs and closed-end credit funds are externally managed under contracts that tie base fees to gross assets—including borrowed capital—rather than market capitalization. Buying back shares shrinks the asset base and permanently cuts the manager’s fee stream, whereas originating loans preserves or grows it.

Even well-aligned managers encounter severe structural hurdles when discounts reach 50%, a level that usually signals credit distress and investor skepticism toward stated NAV. BDCs operate under strict statutory asset-coverage limits and lender covenants; spending cash on buybacks reduces equity while leaving debt unchanged, immediately spiking leverage ratios and risking covenant breaches or credit downgrades. Simultaneously, liquidity tightens as private loan repayments slow, forcing funds to conserve cash for unfunded borrower commitments, upcoming debt maturities, and mandatory dividend distributions. Finally, dislocated markets often offer attractive spreads on new loans, whereas halting originations alienates private equity sponsors who rely on consistent lending capacity and leaves fixed operating costs spread across a smaller, less liquid fund.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Mostly because the manager's incentives and the fund's constraints both favor growing, even though the math favors buying back shares. Buying $1 of NAV for 50 cents is an immediate, certain gain for shareholders, and very few new loans can match that.

The first reason is fees. External managers usually earn base fees on gross assets and incentive fees on income. Buybacks shrink the asset base and the manager's revenue, while new loans grow both.

The second is leverage. Buybacks reduce equity, which raises the debt-to-equity ratio and pushes the fund toward the 1940 Act's 150% asset-coverage minimum and its lender covenants. Some credit agreements limit buybacks outright.

The third is liquidity. Loans are hard to sell at their marks, and the fund often owes cash on unfunded revolvers and delayed-draw commitments. Spare cash tends to go to those obligations.

The fourth is franchise value. Managers want to stay relevant to private-equity sponsors, keep their team, and stay big enough for index inclusion and trading liquidity.

Finally, many managers believe the market is wrong, while investors often suspect the NAV marks are stale. A 50% discount usually signals that investors doubt the stated values or the governance. That doubt is why activists push for buybacks, tender offers, or liquidation.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer: Buying back shares at a 50% discount to NAV is mathematically far more accretive to NAV per share than originating new loans, yet managers rarely do it aggressively because of misaligned incentives and structural constraints. Most BDCs and closed-end credit funds are externally managed and charge base fees on gross assets rather than market capitalization. Repurchasing shares shrinks the equity base and, by extension, the fund's borrowing capacity and total assets, permanently cutting the manager's fee stream. Beyond self-interest, regulatory leverage limits under the Investment Company Act and bank credit-facility covenants tie borrowing capacity to net equity; spending cash on buybacks raises leverage ratios and risks breaching asset-coverage rules or minimum-NAV covenants, especially when a steep discount signals potential upcoming credit write-downs. Finally, credit funds hold illiquid loans alongside unfunded borrower commitments, so preserving cash for liquidity, dividends, and existing sponsor relationships often takes priority over shrinking a fund whose smaller float and higher fixed-expense ratio could widen the discount even further.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
At a 50% discount, every 50 cents spent on buybacks retires a share with $1 of reported NAV, increasing NAV per remaining share. If the loan marks are credible and the fund has spare cash, that can be a better use of capital than originating another loan.

The catch is that NAV is an estimate, and private loans can be hard to sell at their stated values. Buybacks use liquidity the fund may need to meet existing lending commitments, service debt, or stay within leverage limits. New loans can also replace income as older loans pay off, helping sustain distributions.

Incentives matter, too. Many external managers earn fees based on assets. Buybacks shrink the fee base, while originations can maintain or grow it. So the same decision can reflect prudent liquidity management, a conflict of interest, or both. The telling question is how the board justifies using genuinely excess cash for new loans when the fund can buy its own portfolio exposure at half of reported NAV.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
A buyback at 50 cents per dollar of NAV immediately raises NAV per remaining share, assuming the loans are worth their marks. But it also uses cash and shrinks the fund. A new loan can earn interest, replace a loan that repaid, and help sustain distributions. Managers paid on gross assets or investment income may also earn more by keeping capital invested, even when a buyback would create more value for shareholders.

The fund’s balance sheet matters, too. A buyback reduces equity and raises leverage if debt stays constant. Cash may be needed for existing loan commitments, and a credit facility may finance eligible new loans while restricting share repurchases. The discount can also reflect expected credit losses, making the apparent bargain smaller.

If the marks are credible and the fund has surplus cash and room under its leverage limits, buying back shares at half of NAV sets a high bar for any new loan.
